units.description: Glob works on characters (Unicode code points), not bytes, and cancho text is bytes in UTF-8. Return the code point of the character that STARTS at byte index `at` of s (the caller guarantees 0 <= at < len(s) and that `at` is the first byte of a character). Use std.utf8 (utf8.decode gives the code point and the width, or an Invalid step). If the bytes at `at` are not valid UTF-8, return 0x110000 plus that byte's value, so a malformed byte never equals any real pattern character. Must never panic.

The width in BYTES of the character that starts at byte index `at` of s (same preconditions as glob_cp_at): 1 for ASCII, 2 for "é", up to 4. For a malformed byte it is the width utf8.decode reports for the invalid step, and it is always at least 1, so a loop that advances by it always makes progress. Must never panic.

units.signature: fn glob_set_has[&r](pat: &r [byte], s: int, e: int, c: int) -> [] int
units.description: Work on the BODY of a bracket set: the bytes pat[s..e), which is what lies between "[" (or "[!") and the closing "]", and is not empty. c is a code point. Items of the body are read left to right: "x-y" (a character, a dash, a character, with the dash neither first nor last in the body) is a range from x to y inclusive by code point; any other character is a plain one and stands for itself, a first or last "-" included, and backslash is just a character here. Return 1 if c is in the set, 0 if it is not, and -1 if the body holds a range with x greater than y (a reversed range makes the whole set invalid, even when c would not have been in it, so scan the whole body). Characters are code points, not bytes: use glob_cp_at and glob_cp_len. This only answers membership: the "!" negation and the rule that no set matches "/" belong to the caller.
tests: pub fn test_set_dash_last() -> [] int { test.assert_eq(glob_set_has("a-", 0, 2, 45), 1); test.assert_eq(glob_set_has("a-", 0, 2, 98), 0); return 0; }
pub fn test_set_dash_first() -> [] int { test.assert_eq(glob_set_has("-a", 0, 2, 45), 1); return 0; }
pub fn test_set_two_ranges() -> [] int { test.assert_eq(glob_set_has("a-cx-z", 0, 6, 121), 1); test.assert_eq(glob_set_has("a-cx-z", 0, 6, 100), 0); return 0; }
pub fn test_set_reversed_late() -> [] int { test.assert_eq(glob_set_has("ab-z9-0", 0, 7, 97), -1); return 0; }
pub fn test_set_subrange_of_longer_text() -> [] int { test.assert_eq(glob_set_has("[x-z]!", 1, 4, 121), 1); test.assert_eq(glob_set_has("[x-z]!", 1, 4, 33), 0); return 0; }
pub fn test_set_utf8() -> [] int { test.assert_eq(glob_set_has("é-ü", 0, 5, 233), 1); test.assert_eq(glob_set_has("é-ü", 0, 5, 97), 0); return 0; }

units.description: Split a pattern into tokens: given a pattern and an index p with 0 <= p < len(pat) at the START of a token, return the index just after that token, or -1 if the token is malformed. Tokens: "**" (two stars) is one token, ending at p+2; a single "*" ends at p+1; "?" ends at p+1; a backslash followed by any character is one token covering both (the character may be several bytes), and a backslash that is the last byte of the pattern is malformed (-1); "[" starts a set that runs to the FIRST "]" after the optional "!" and ends just after that "]"; it is malformed (-1) if there is no "]" at all, if the set is empty (the "]" comes straight after "[" or "[!"), or if glob_set_has says -1 for its body. Any other character is a token by itself, as wide as that character is in bytes.
tests: pub fn test_tok_single_star() -> [] int { test.assert_eq(glob_tok_end("*a", 0), 1); test.assert_eq(glob_tok_end("*", 0), 1); return 0; }
pub fn test_tok_escape() -> [] int { test.assert_eq(glob_tok_end("\\*b", 0), 2); test.assert_eq(glob_tok_end("\\é", 0), 3); return 0; }
pub fn test_tok_set_negated() -> [] int { test.assert_eq(glob_tok_end("[!a]", 0), 4); return 0; }
pub fn test_tok_set_empty() -> [] int { test.assert_eq(glob_tok_end("[]", 0), -1); test.assert_eq(glob_tok_end("[!]", 0), -1); return 0; }
pub fn test_tok_set_reversed() -> [] int { test.assert_eq(glob_tok_end("[z-a]", 0), -1); return 0; }
pub fn test_tok_wide_literal() -> [] int { test.assert_eq(glob_tok_end("éa", 0), 2); return 0; }

units.description: Whether the pattern is well formed: true exactly when walking it token by token with glob_tok_end never meets a malformed token (-1). The empty pattern is valid. A pattern is invalid if a "[" is never closed, a set is empty ("[]", "[!]", and so "[]a]" too: the first "]" closes the set), a range has its first character above its second, or the pattern ends with a single unpaired backslash. Must never panic, on any bytes.
tests: pub fn test_valid_ex1() -> [] int { test.assert(glob_valid("*.txt")); return 0; }
pub fn test_valid_ex2() -> [] int { test.assert(glob_valid("")); return 0; }
pub fn test_valid_ex3() -> [] int { test.assert(!glob_valid("[abc")); return 0; }
pub fn test_valid_ex4() -> [] int { test.assert(!glob_valid("[]")); return 0; }
pub fn test_valid_ex5() -> [] int { test.assert(!glob_valid("a\\")); return 0; }

units.signature: fn glob_one[&r](pat: &r [byte], p: int, c: int) -> [] bool
units.description: Does the ONE-character token that starts at index p of the (valid) pattern accept the code point c? The token at p is not a star: it is "?", a backslash escape, a "[...]" set, or a plain character. "?" accepts any c except "/" (47). A plain character accepts only itself, and "\\x" accepts only x (the escaped character), so both of them DO accept "/" when that is the character written. A set accepts c if c is in it (glob_set_has returns 1) and c is not "/"; a set that starts with "!" is negated and accepts c if c is not in the set (glob_set_has returns 0) and c is not "/". No set ever accepts "/", negated or not.
tests: pub fn test_one_ex1() -> [] int { test.assert(glob_one("?", 0, 97)); return 0; }
pub fn test_one_ex2() -> [] int { test.assert(!glob_one("?", 0, 47)); return 0; }
pub fn test_one_ex3() -> [] int { test.assert(glob_one("a", 0, 97)); return 0; }
pub fn test_one_ex4() -> [] int { test.assert(glob_one("[!a-c]", 0, 100)); return 0; }
pub fn test_one_ex5() -> [] int { test.assert(!glob_one("[!a-c]", 0, 98)); return 0; }

pub fn test_one_slash_rules() -> [] int { test.assert(!glob_one("[!a]", 0, 47)); test.assert(!glob_one("[/]", 0, 47)); test.assert(glob_one("/", 0, 47)); test.assert(glob_one("\\/", 0, 47)); return 0; }
pub fn test_one_escape() -> [] int { test.assert(glob_one("\\*", 0, 42)); test.assert(!glob_one("\\*", 0, 97)); return 0; }
pub fn test_one_offset() -> [] int { test.assert(glob_one("xy[ab]", 2, 98)); test.assert(!glob_one("xy[ab]", 2, 99)); return 0; }
pub fn test_one_utf8() -> [] int { test.assert(glob_one("é", 0, 233)); test.assert(!glob_one("é", 0, 101)); return 0; }

units.description: Whether the WHOLE text matches the pattern; an invalid pattern (glob_valid false) matches nothing. "*" matches zero or more characters, none of them "/"; "**" (two stars in a row) matches zero or more characters of any kind, including "/" (it has no special handling of slashes around it: "a/**/b" matches "a/x/y/b" but not "a/b"); "?" matches exactly one character that is not "/"; sets, escapes and plain characters are exactly what glob_one decides. A character is a code point, not a byte: "?" matches "é" and "??" does not. The empty pattern matches only the empty text. It must be fast: "a*a*a*a*b" against 25 letters "a" must return false at once, with no exponential backtracking. Do not recurse over the text: walk the pattern token by token (glob_tok_end) and keep, in an arena region, a table over the byte offsets of the text (n + 1 entries, a slice made with alloc_slice) saying which offsets the tokens so far can have consumed up to; offsets that fall in the middle of a multi-byte character are never set. Never panics, on any bytes.
tests: pub fn test_match_ex1() -> [] int { test.assert(glob_match("*.txt", "a.txt")); return 0; }
pub fn test_match_ex2() -> [] int { test.assert(!glob_match("*.txt", "a/b.txt")); return 0; }
pub fn test_match_ex3() -> [] int { test.assert(glob_match("**.txt", "a/b.txt")); return 0; }
pub fn test_match_ex4() -> [] int { test.assert(glob_match("a?c", "abc")); return 0; }
pub fn test_match_ex5() -> [] int { test.assert(glob_match("?", "é")); return 0; }
pub fn test_match_ex6() -> [] int { test.assert(!glob_match("??", "é")); return 0; }
pub fn test_match_ex7() -> [] int { test.assert(!glob_match("[a-c]x", "dx")); return 0; }
pub fn test_match_ex8() -> [] int { test.assert(!glob_match("[abc", "a")); return 0; }
pub fn test_match_ex9() -> [] int { test.assert(glob_match("", "")); return 0; }
pub fn test_match_double_star_slashes() -> [] int { test.assert(glob_match("x/**/y", "x/p/q/y")); test.assert(!glob_match("x/**/y", "x/y")); test.assert(glob_match("x/**", "x/p/q")); return 0; }
pub fn test_match_star_stops_at_slash() -> [] int { test.assert(!glob_match("*", "p/q")); test.assert(glob_match("*", "")); test.assert(glob_match("p/*", "p/")); return 0; }
pub fn test_match_set_and_negation() -> [] int { test.assert(glob_match("[!a]", "b")); test.assert(!glob_match("[!a]", "/")); test.assert(glob_match("[a-]", "-")); return 0; }
pub fn test_match_escape() -> [] int { test.assert(glob_match("a\\*b", "a*b")); test.assert(!glob_match("a\\*b", "axb")); return 0; }
pub fn test_match_whole_text() -> [] int { test.assert(!glob_match("ab", "abc")); test.assert(!glob_match("bc", "abc")); test.assert(!glob_match("", "a")); return 0; }
pub fn test_match_no_blowup() -> [] int { test.assert(!glob_match("a*a*a*b", "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa")); return 0; }
pub fn test_match_utf8_count() -> [] int { test.assert(glob_match("??", "éè")); test.assert(!glob_match("?", "éè")); return 0; }
